title: When Machine Lanes Break the Cloud

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: Welcome back, everyone! Today we're diving into a story that sounds like a cyber thriller—except it's real. A build pipeline went dark, not because of a crash or a bug, but because a virtual machine was waiting for a human to log into a browser in California.

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: Exactly. It’s a perfect example of what happens when you let autonomous systems depend on human-facing infrastructure. The orchestrator and the conductor were on the same machine—same motherboard, same power supply—but one was a Windows process, the other a Linux VM in Hyper-V.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So they were literally next to each other, but couldn’t talk? That feels like a digital version of two people in the same room but unable to hear each other because one’s on a phone call with someone in another country.

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: That’s the core irony. They were using Tailscale—an encrypted overlay network that’s brilliant for humans on the move. But when you point a headless build agent at it, you’re asking it to do something it wasn’t designed for: authenticate without a browser, without a keyboard, without a human.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So Tailscale’s security features—like 180-day key expiry and browser re-authentication—became the enemy. It’s like putting a password lock on a vending machine that’s supposed to work 24/7.

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: Exactly. That’s why ADR-0014 was born: Machine lanes don’t ride the tailnet. The rule is simple: human traffic—laptops, phones, operator consoles—can use Tailscale. But machines? They need local, stable, predictable networking.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So what’s the alternative? Local metal, right? Sibling DNS, static IPs, direct Ethernet connections.

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: Yes. But even local networks have their own demons. Take Hyper-V’s Default Switch. It’s convenient—it gives VMs internet access and auto-registers them in mshome.net. But here’s the catch: it changes its subnet every reboot.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So the VM gets a new IP address every time the host restarts? That sounds like a nightmare for automation.

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: It is. In July, the subnet was 172.19.240.0/20. August? 172.29.64.0/20. September? 172.17.192.0/20. The VMs get new IPs via DHCP, DNS updates, but SSH doesn’t know the host key changed. In interactive mode, it warns you. In BatchMode? It just fails silently with return code 255.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So the build pipeline crashes because a machine’s IP changed—but no one noticed because the DNS updated and the SSH client didn’t complain.

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: Exactly. The fix? In ~/.ssh/config, you must set StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new. That way, if a host key is new, it’s automatically accepted. No human needed. No queue backlog.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: And then there’s the loopback wall. I love that phrase. So even if a service is running on 127.0.0.1, the VM can’t reach it.

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: Yes. The host’s loopback is isolated from the VM’s virtual network. So when the builder VM tried to reach the inference server on port 8082, it got connection refused. The solution? Point it to a physical machine on the same LAN—fx99 at 192.168.12.220.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So even though the hypervisor has two B70 GPUs, the VMs can’t use them because of network topology. The hardware specs don’t matter if the plumbing’s broken.

turns.speaker: host_b
turns.text: That’s the punchline. Machine lanes need reachable addresses, stable routing, and autonomous key negotiation. Until you solve the network, your hardware is just expensive paperweights.

turns.speaker: host_a
turns.text: So the takeaway? Build systems aren’t just about code and compute. They’re about network design. And sometimes, the most powerful machine is the one that stays local.
